text: ASD-STE100 was developed by AECMA (European Association of Aerospace Industries), which later became part of ASD.
The AECMA Simplified English Working Group was formally established on 30 June 1983 in Amsterdam.
The first public release of the AECMA Simplified English Guide was in 1986, with document number PSC-85-16598.
There was a pre-release Issue 0 in 1985 before the first public Issue 1 in 1986.
The organizational rename from AECMA to ASD occurred in 2004, and the first issue released under the ASD-STE100 title appeared in 2005.
The current issue of ASD-STE100 is Issue 9, dated 15 January 2025, and it is now designated an international standard.
Issue 9 consists of 53 writing rules and a dictionary of approximately 900 approved words.
ASD-STE100 is maintained by the ASD Simplified Technical English Maintenance Group (STEMG).
ASD-STE100 is distributed free of charge but is not open-licensed; unauthorized redistribution is prohibited without written permission.
The Aerospace Industries Association of America (AIA) collaborated with AECMA in developing STE.
The key driver for creating STE was a request from airlines (approximately 80% of which were not from English-speaking countries) to ensure accurate maintenance practices and aircraft safety.
Fokker's involvement in STE's founding is documented because the first working group meeting was held at the Fokker plant near Schiphol Airport.
Douglas/McDonnell Douglas involvement in founding STE cannot be sourced from authoritative primary materials.
ASD-STE100 is explicitly not intended for general-purpose writing.

STE's current popularity in AI and tooling circles derives from its machine-operability—its rules are easy to encode as checklists, constraints, and linters—rather than from fitness for general prose.
STE is actively harmful for persuasion because it removes by design the devices persuasion depends on, such as metaphor, cadence variation, rhetorical questions, and unhedged voice.
The Hemingway Editor uses the Automated Readability Index (ARI) to compute its grade-level score.
Hemingway Editor's own materials acknowledge that grade level does not define the target audience, yet the product UI trains users to lower the number anyway.
Hotaling (2020) is a craft-consensus essay for scientific writers, not an empirical study; it explicitly warns against over-condensing into unclarity.
Hotaling (2020) cites Gopen & Swan (1990) and Williams & Bizup as foundational references.

The claude-writing-skills repository's `humanize` skill includes explicit academic overrides that protect calibrated hedges, passive voice when the agent is irrelevant, and Gopen & Swan stress/topic positions.
The `humanize` skill's cadence CV threshold of greater than 0.4 is a heuristic with no empirical grounding.
The AI-tell catalog in the `humanize` skill rests on community-maintained practitioner consensus (e.g., Wikipedia's 'Signs of AI writing' page) rather than validated experimental studies.

Rule-list and readability-formula tools share the assumption that writing quality has surface features detectable without a full model of the reader's goal, but this assumption is only partially supported—valid as a diagnostic, not as an optimization target.
Optimizing a readability formula score can produce prose that scores well but says nothing meaningful—a Goodhart's Law problem.
ASD-STE100 Issue 9 grants irrevocable, free-of-charge special usage rights to specific categories including ASD member companies, AIA members, universities, and airworthiness authorities.
ASD-STE100 was granted the European Union Trade Mark in 2006 and again in 2018.
In 1987, ATA included a requirement to write in STE in ATA100.
The `claude-writing-skills` STE skill is a lossy compression of the official standard because it encodes rules but not the full controlled dictionary, which is restricted by copyright.
A blank voice-profile in the `humanize` skill produces generic de-slopped prose rather than the specific author's voice.
STEMG's own training material states that STE is not a simplified version of English for the writers, only for the readers.
No strong empirical outcome studies (e.g., RCTs showing STE improves comprehension, error reduction, or safety outcomes) were found in open sources.
Issue 10 of ASD-STE100 is scheduled for January 2028.
Gopen & Swan (1990) is drawn from reading-comprehension research and focuses on topic position, stress position, old-to-new flow, and subject-verb proximity.
